title: 2 Timothy

stories.title: 📜 2 Timothy 1
summaryBullets: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, (1:1).
To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. (1:2).
I thank God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as did my forefathers, as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers. (1:3).
Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy. (1:4).
I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well. (1:5).
For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. (1:6).
For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control. (1:7).
So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God. (1:8).
He has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began. (1:9).
And now He has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel, (1:10).
to which I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher. (1:11).
For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day. (1:12).
Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. (1:13).
Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. (1:14).
You know that everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes. (1:15).
May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. (1:16).
Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me. (1:17).
May the Lord grant Onesiphorus His mercy on that day. You know very well how much he ministered to me in Ephesus. (1:18).
crossRefs: 1 Timothy 4:14: Gift given by laying on of hands.
Romans 8:15: Spirit of adoption, not fear.
Titus 1:3: Paul entrusted as preacher and apostle.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִצִּית אֵשׁ (hiṣṣît ʾēš, sense), Greek: ἀναζωπυρεῖν (anazōpýrein, NT), Aramaic: אֲזָרֵי נוּרָא (ʾazarē nūrā, sense)
translationNotes.note: Means to rekindle or stir up fire; figurative for cultivating and exercising a spiritual gift.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פִּקָּדוֹן (piqqādōn), Greek: παραθήκη (parathḗkē, NT), Aramaic: פקדנא (paqdanā)
translationNotes.note: Refers to something entrusted for safekeeping; here, the gospel message and ministry charge.

Rome did not feed or clothe men held for trial. The state supplied the cell and the guard; food, clothing, bedding, and anything else came from whoever on the outside was willing to bring it. A prisoner in military custody was commonly chained by the wrist to the soldier watching him, which is what Paul means in Acts 28:20 by 'I am bound with this chain'. That is the practical work Onesiphorus was doing when he 'often refreshed me' in 1:16.

translationNotes.term: Onesiphorus searched until he found me
translationNotes.note: Rome had no street numbers, no public list of who was being held where, and no way to look a prisoner up. A man arriving from Asia Minor had to work the city by hand, quarter by quarter, asking after a foreigner held on a capital charge. Doing that in the open also tied his own name to that charge, which is why Paul says twice that he 'was unashamed of my chains' (1:16). He had already served Paul at Ephesus (1:18), and Paul greets his household again in 4:19.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul thanks God for Timothy’s faith, urges courage and faithfulness in guarding the gospel, and recalls examples of desertion and loyalty.

stories.title: 🌿 2 Timothy 2
summaryBullets: You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. (2:1).
And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well. (2:2).
Join me in suffering, like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. (2:3).
A soldier refrains from entangling himself in civilian affairs, in order to please the one who enlisted him. (2:4).
Likewise, a competitor does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules. (2:5).
The hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops. (2:6).
Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things. (2:7).
Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel, (2:8).
for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained! (2:9).
For this reason I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory. (2:10).
This is a trustworthy saying: If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; (2:11).
if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; (2:12).
if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself. (2:13).
Remind the believers of these things, charging them before God to avoid quarreling over words, which succeeds only in leading the listeners to ruin. (2:14).
Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth. (2:15).
But avoid irreverent, empty chatter, which will only lead to more ungodliness, (2:16).
and the talk of such men will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, (2:17).
who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some. (2:18).
Nevertheless, God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.” (2:19).
A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay. Some indeed are for honorable use, but others are for common use. (2:20).
So if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work. (2:21).
Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. (2:22).
But reject foolish and ignorant speculation, for you know that it breeds quarreling. (2:23).
And a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing. (2:24).
He must gently reprove those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth. (2:25).
Then they will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will. (2:26).
crossRefs: 1 Corinthians 9:24-27: Competing for an imperishable crown.
Titus 1:9: Holding firm to the trustworthy word.

translationNotes.term: Rightly handle the word of truth
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָשַׁר בַּדָּבָר (yāšar baddāḇār, sense), Greek: ὀρθοτομεῖν τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας (orthotomeîn ton lógon tēs alētheías, NT), Aramaic: פשיט מלתא דקושטא (pəšīṭ milṯā d-quštā, sense)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'cut straight'; figurative for teaching and applying God’s word correctly.

A Roman legionary swore the sacramentum, the military oath binding him to his commander, and served a fixed term of twenty years. During that service he was barred by law from contracting a legal marriage, and he was kept out of trade and landholding where he was stationed. That is the exact force of 2:4: a soldier who takes on civilian business is a soldier who has divided himself, and Paul assumes his reader knows what enlistment cost a man.

The Greek games ran on sworn rules. At Olympia every competitor swore an oath before a statue of Zeus that he had trained for the required ten months and would break no regulation, and the judges could flog and fine men who cheated. Pausanias, writing in the second century, describes the row of bronze Zeus statues at the entrance to the stadium that were paid for out of those fines and inscribed with the cheats' names, so that every athlete walked past them on the way in (Description of Greece 5.21).

A medical term, and this is the only place it occurs in the New Testament. Gangrene is flesh dying and rotting while the body is still alive, and it does not stay put; it eats outward through the surrounding tissue. Ancient physicians had one treatment, which was to cut the dead flesh away or take the limb off. Paul chose a word his readers would have heard from a doctor, not a preacher.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul urges Timothy to endure hardship, pass on the gospel, avoid quarrels, and correct with gentleness, using soldier, athlete, and farmer metaphors.

stories.title: 📜 2 Timothy 3
summaryBullets: But understand this: In the last days terrible times will come. (3:1).
For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, (3:2).
unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, without love of good, (3:3).
traitorous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, (3:4).
having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such as these! (3:5).
They are the kind who worm their way into households and captivate vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and led astray by various passions, (3:6).
who are always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth. (3:7).
Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth. They are depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith. (3:8).
But they will not advance much further. For just like Jannes and Jambres, their folly will be plain to everyone. (3:9).
You, however, have observed my teaching, my conduct, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my perseverance, (3:10).
my persecutions, and the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. What persecutions I endured! Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them. (3:11).
Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, (3:12).
while evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived. (3:13).
But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. (3:14).
From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. (3:15).
All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, (3:16).
so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work. (3:17).
crossRefs: Matthew 24:12: Lawlessness and love growing cold.
2 Peter 1:21: Men spoke from God as carried by the Spirit.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים (ʾaḥarīt hayyāmîm), Greek: ἐσχάται ἡμέραι (eschátai hēmérai, NT), Aramaic: יומיא דסופא (yōmayā d-sūfā)
translationNotes.note: Phrase for the final period of history; in NT it refers to the time inaugurated by Christ leading to his return.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִשְׁמַת אֱלוֹהַּ (nišmat ʾĕlōah, sense), Greek: θεόπνευστος (theópneustos, NT), Aramaic: נפיחת אלהא (nəpīḥaṯ ʾAlāhā, sense)
translationNotes.note: Unique word meaning 'breathed out by God'; used of Scripture’s divine origin.

Exodus does not give the names of the Egyptian magicians who matched Aaron's signs and then failed at the gnats (Exodus 7:11-12, 7:22, 8:7, 8:18-19). Paul names two of them. Those names were in circulation in Jewish writing of the period: the Damascus Document, found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, sets Jannes and his brother against Moses and Aaron, and Pliny the Elder lists a Jannes among the Egyptian names attached to magic (Natural History 30.11).

Three cities in the Roman province of Galatia, in the middle of what is now Turkey, and the exact route of Paul's first journey in Acts 13-14. He was driven out of Pisidian Antioch, a Roman colony on the high plateau, then out of Iconium, and at Lystra he was stoned, dragged outside the city, and left for dead (Acts 14:19). Lystra was Timothy's own town (Acts 16:1-2), so Paul is not citing distant history to him; he is naming Timothy's street.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul warns of corrupt people in the last days, recalls his example of endurance, and affirms the divine inspiration and usefulness of all Scripture.

stories.title: 🌿 2 Timothy 4
summaryBullets: I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His appearing and His kingdom: (4:1).
Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction. (4:2).
For the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires. (4:3).
So they will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths. (4:4).
But you, be sober in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry. (4:5).
For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. (4:6).
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. (4:7).
From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day — and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing. (4:8).
Make every effort to come to me quickly, (4:9).
because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. (4:10).
Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry. (4:11).
Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus. (4:12).
When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments. (4:13).
Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. (4:14).
You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message. (4:15).
At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. (4:16).
But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion. (4:17).
And the Lord will rescue me from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom. To Him be the glory forever and ever. Amen. (4:18).
Greet Prisca and Aquila, as well as the household of Onesiphorus. (4:19).
Erastus has remained at Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus. (4:20).
Make every effort to come to me before winter. Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers. (4:21).
The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all. (4:22).
crossRefs: 1 Corinthians 9:24: Run to obtain the prize.
Philippians 3:14: Press on toward the prize.
James 1:12: Crown of life promised to those who love him.

translationNotes.term: Fight the good fight / finish the race
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לָחַם מִלְחָמָה / כִּלָּה מֵרוֹץ (lāḥam milḥāmāh / killāh mērōṣ, sense); Greek: τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα ἠγώνισμαι / τὸν δρόμον τετέλεκα (ton kalòn agōna ēgṓnismai / ton drómon tetéleka, NT); Aramaic: קרבא טבא קרבית / רהטא שלמת (qarbā ṭābā qarēḇt / rahaṭā šlemṯ, sense)
translationNotes.note: Athletic and military metaphors for faithful perseverance and completion of one’s mission.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲטֶרֶת צְדָקָה (ʿăṭéret ṣədāqāh, sense), Greek: ὁ τῆς δικαιοσύνης στέφανος (ho tēs dikaiosýnēs stéphanos, NT), Aramaic: כלילא דזדקתא (kelīlā d-zidqātā)
translationNotes.note: Reward imagery for the faithful; crown symbolizes honor and vindication given at Christ’s appearing.

translationNotes.term: The cloak, the scrolls, and the parchments
translationNotes.note: The phailones was a heavy circular travelling cloak of thick wool with a hole cut for the head, worn against rain and slept under on the road. Paul is in a cell asking for it before winter (4:21). The scrolls are papyrus; the parchments are membranai, a Latin word for prepared animal skin, which cost far more than papyrus, took a flock to produce, lasted for generations, and took ink on both sides. Troas is the port of Alexandria Troas on the Aegean coast, the crossing point to Macedonia (Acts 16:8-11).

Apologia is the formal answer an accused man made in court, speaking for himself. Roman practice expected a defendant to appear supported by friends and patrons who stood with him in the room, since their public backing was itself evidence of his character. Paul says no one stood with him. The phrase 'the mouth of the lion' in 4:17 is drawn from Psalm 22:21, 'Save me from the mouth of the lion'.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul charges Timothy to preach faithfully, reflects on finishing his course and awaiting a crown, recounts personal companions and hardships, and closes with greetings and blessing.

intro:
2 Timothy was written by Paul the apostle (2 Timothy 1:1), the second of the Pastoral Epistles and the last letter Paul ever wrote, composed from the Mamertine Prison in Rome around AD 66-67, only weeks or months before his execution by beheading under the emperor Nero. Unlike the relatively comfortable two-year house arrest of Paul's first Roman imprisonment (AD 60-62, the end of Acts), this second imprisonment was severe: Paul was held in chains (2 Timothy 1:16; 2:9) in a dungeon and was on trial in a capital case in which conviction was essentially certain. The Great Fire of Rome (July 18-19, AD 64) had destroyed two-thirds of the city; the emperor Nero, suspected of having ordered the fire himself to clear ground for his new palace, deflected popular blame onto the Christians and launched the empire's first organized persecution of the Christian church (the Roman historian Tacitus describes Nero's vicious treatment of Christians in Annals 15.44, written c. AD 116). Paul had been re-arrested somewhere in the eastern empire (probably at Troas, where he left his cloak and parchments, 2 Timothy 4:13) and transported back to Rome for trial. The traditional site of his imprisonment is the Mamertine Prison (Latin Tullianum or Carcer Tullianum), the underground dungeon at the base of the Capitoline Hill on the edge of the Roman Forum where political prisoners awaiting execution were held; both Peter and Paul are traditionally held to have been imprisoned there during Nero's persecution. The letter is intensely personal and valedictory in tone. Paul knows he is about to die: "I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day" (2 Timothy 4:6-8). Most of his coworkers have left him: "Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me" (4:10-11). He asks Timothy to come quickly to Rome, bringing Mark with him ("he is very useful to me for ministry," 4:11, marking Mark's full reconciliation with Paul after the rift of Acts 15:36-40) and bringing his cloak and his books and parchments from Troas (4:13). Whether Timothy reached Paul before Paul's execution is unknown. Paul (originally Saul) was born in Tarsus of Cilicia around AD 5-10 to a Hebrew family of the tribe of Benjamin, educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel the Pharisee before his conversion on the Damascus road and his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles; he was martyred by beheading in Rome under Nero around AD 66-67 (see the introduction to Romans for the full biographical sketch).

The historical setting is the city of Rome in the final years of Nero's reign and the early years of the Neronian persecution of Christians. Nero (born AD 37, reigned AD 54-68) had become emperor at age sixteen after the death of his stepfather and adoptive father Claudius (whom his mother Agrippina the Younger had poisoned to clear Nero's path to the throne). The early years of his reign (AD 54-62) had been remarkably stable and well-governed under the influence of his Stoic tutor Seneca and the praetorian prefect Sextus Afranius Burrus; these years saw the period when Paul's first Roman imprisonment ended with his release. By the mid-60s, however, Nero had murdered his mother (AD 59), his wife Octavia (AD 62), and Burrus (AD 62, possibly poisoned), forced Seneca's retirement and later his suicide (AD 65), and given himself over to public musical performances and increasingly erratic behavior. The Great Fire of Rome in July AD 64 destroyed ten of the city's fourteen districts; Nero began rebuilding with grand public works (and a vast new palace for himself called the Domus Aurea, "Golden House"), and selected Christians as scapegoats for the fire. Tacitus describes the persecution: "Besides being put to death they [the Christians] were made to serve as objects of amusement; they were clothed in the hides of beasts and torn to pieces by dogs; others were crucified, others set on fire to serve to illuminate the night when daylight failed" (Annals 15.44). The traditional location of Paul's imprisonment, the Mamertine Prison, still stands today below the Church of San Giuseppe dei Falegnami at the base of the Capitoline Hill in Rome; the lower chamber (the original Tullianum, dating from the 6th century BC) is preserved and venerated as the site of Peter's and Paul's final imprisonment.

2 Timothy is the fifty-fifth book of the Christian Bible, the sixteenth book of the New Testament, and the eleventh of Paul's thirteen letters in canonical order. The letter has four chapters and is the second of the three Pastoral Epistles. The earliest surviving manuscripts include Codex Sinaiticus (4th century) and Codex Alexandrinus (5th century AD); the Pastoral Epistles are not preserved in Papyrus 46. Several of 2 Timothy's passages have become foundational to Christian doctrine and practice: 2 Timothy 2:15 ("Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth"); 2 Timothy 3:1-9 warns of the moral character of "the last days"; 2 Timothy 3:16-17 is the New Testament's most explicit statement on the nature of Scripture ("All Scripture is breathed out by God [Greek theopneustos] and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be competent, equipped for every good work"); and 2 Timothy 4:1-8 contains Paul's final charge to Timothy ("Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching") and his own valedictory testimony ("I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith").
